notes.SF: Zetkin built a separate women's section of the SPD, but Marxists insist on joint class struggle with men: +1.
notes.LIF: NOW and suffrage societies included men and women; Friedan accepted women's groups but not as a rule: +1.
notes.NAS: Falange had a Sección Femenina under state direction, not an independent women's rights movement: -1.

trade.selfreliance.6.why: Local production at higher cost is localist and autarkic, favoured by agrarian, communitarian and nationalist camps and opposed by commercial and technological-abundance ones.

notes.HF: Hamilton's commercial republic relies on wide markets and the specialisation of trade: -2.
notes.TRA: Abundance through global technology and AI is the transhumanist route, not higher-cost localism: -2.
notes.CO: Communitarians favour local economies and rootedness (MacIntyre's local communities), though not strictly: +1.
notes.STC: Salazar's rural, frugal, near-autarkic Portugal valued self-sufficiency: +1.

distribution.labour.9.why: Right-to-work: libertarian voluntarism rejects compulsory union membership, while corporatist and syndicalist regimes make membership of state-run syndicates compulsory.

notes.STC: Estado Novo's Statute of National Labour set compulsory state-controlled sindicatos nacionais: -3.
notes.NAS: Falange's vertical syndicates enrolled all workers and employers under state authority: -3.
notes.CRA: Voluntary association is absolute for cypherpunks: +3.
notes.IS: Vargas-era Brazil made union tax (imposto sindical) compulsory, and CEPAL-style developmentalism leaned on organised labour: -2.

identity.culture.1.why: Whether a pure national identity needs shielding: nationalist and civilisationist camps say yes, liberal, left and tech camps say identities are hybrid.

notes.NAS: Falange's 'unity of destiny in the universal' and Hispanidad make national essence the first principle: -3.
notes.EUR: Eurasianism is built on a distinct civilisation to be defended from Western liberal influence (Trubetskoy's Europe and Mankind): -3.
notes.STC: Estado Novo's Chúa, Tổ quốc, Gia đình stressed protecting national and Catholic tradition: -2.
notes.TRA: Transhumanists think beyond nation and species; Huxley and Hughes hold cosmopolitan views: +2.

liberty.justice.8.1: CO LIF SF TRA CRA PIP
liberty.justice.8.why: Replacing prison with community service, reconciliation or treatment divides liberal and restorative camps from order-first authoritarian and traditionalist ones.

notes.STC: Estado Novo relied on prisons, the PIDE and 'security measures' against dissidents and offenders: -2.
notes.CO: Etzioni's responsive communitarianism and restorative justice, with community and victim reconciliation, are congenial: +1.
notes.RF: MacKinnon and Dworkin want firm punishment for sexual violence, against lenient alternatives: -1.
notes.HF: Federalists favoured firm enforcement and punishment, defending Whiskey Rebellion prosecutions and sedition law: -2.

trade.capital.5.why: Whether multinationals drain poor countries: dependency-minded, nationalist and anti-Western camps say yes; commercial and libertarian camps say they bring capital.

notes.IS: Prebisch's centre-periphery analysis sees foreign firms extracting rents, yet Kubitschek courted foreign auto and steel investors, so only a mild lean: +1.
notes.NAS: Falange's 27 points attack finance capital and foreign economic domination: +2.
notes.HF: Hamilton wanted foreign capital for American industry and credit: -2.
notes.SUL: Somoza, Marcos and Mobutu partnered with foreign firms and shared the proceeds: -1.

distribution.welfare.1.1: COA CO IS LIF PIP EUR
distribution.welfare.1.why: State-guaranteed free health and education divides left and developmentalist camps from budget-balancing, limited-government and libertarian ones.

notes.SF: Socialising care and reproduction costs through public services is the socialist-feminist programme: +3.
notes.CRA: Cypherpunks reject tax-funded public provision: -3.
notes.STC: Salazar's balanced-budget austerity left health and schooling thin and largely church- or family-based: -1.
notes.NAS: Falange promised social justice and state-guaranteed social services within the national syndicates: +2.
notes.HF: Federalists favoured limited government, with schooling left to states and communities: -1.

economy.planning.8.why: Freedom to set prices without permission is a market-liberal position; corporatist, developmentalist and statist camps want state oversight of prices.

notes.CRA: Untraceable private contracts and pricing are cypherpunk first principles: +3.
notes.STC: Salazar's condicionamento industrial and the corporatist price-fixing boards regulated what firms could do and charge: -2.
notes.HF: Hamilton's commercial republic supported free enterprise under strong credit, with no price boards: +2.
notes.SUL: Rulers grant monopolies and licences to cronies, so pricing is not free of permission: -1.

distribution.tax.11.why: Whether earned wealth is mainly the earner's own: libertarian and property-first camps say yes, redistributive and social-justice camps say society has a claim.

notes.CRA: Untaxable wealth is the cypherpunk goal: +3.
notes.HF: Hamilton and Federalist No. 10 defend property and the fruits of unequal talents: +2.
notes.SF: Socialist feminism holds that profit depends on unpaid care and others' labour: -2.
notes.NAS: Falange's 27 points subordinate private gain to national and social needs: -2.

empire.10.why: Trading territory for peace and statehood is rejected by imperial-nationalist camps and welcomed by liberal and internationalist ones.

notes.EUR: Neo-Eurasianism treats lost borderlands as part of the civilisational space to be regathered: -3.
notes.NAS: Falange's 27 points demand imperial expansion and Spain's 'historic destiny': -3.
notes.LIF: Liberal-democratic politics favours compromise and negotiated settlement over territorial claims: +2.
notes.COA: Milosevic's Serbia fought to hold or expand Serb territory, so adherents lean against concessions: -1.

trade.selfreliance.4.why: Whether closing off is a mistake: open-world liberal, technological and digital camps say yes; autarkic, developmentalist and fortress-civilisation camps accept closing.

notes.STC: Salazar's 'Orgulhosamente sós' (proudly alone) isolation was the Estado Novo's stance: -2.
notes.IS: Substitution strategy withdraws from import dependence to build national industry: -2.
notes.EUR: Eurasianism envisages a closed civilisation bloc against liberal Western influence: -2.
notes.CRA: Borderless communication and trade is the cypherpunk premise: +2.

trade.capital.1.why: Barring foreigners from land, ports and strategic firms is a nationalist-sovereigntist measure favoured by corporatist, developmentalist and Eurasianist camps and rejected by open-capital ones.

notes.EUR: Control of strategic sectors by the national state is a pillar of neo-Eurasian geopolitics: +2.
notes.NAS: Falange's 27 points nationalise banks and protect the national economy against foreign finance: +2.
notes.HF: Hamilton welcomed foreign capital in American canals, banks and industry: -2.
notes.CRA: Nothing in cypherpunk thought allows borders on ownership: -3.

change.pace.6.why: A catch-up sprint compressing a century into years is developmentalism's signature; gradualist and conservative camps are wary.

notes.IS: Kubitschek's slogan 'fifty years of progress in five' is the textbook case: +3.
notes.NAS: Falange called for a national revolution to restore Spain's greatness at speed: +2.
notes.STC: Salazar's Portugal prized stability, frugality and slow organic change: -1.
notes.HF: Hamilton's programme aimed to build credit and manufactures fast so America could stand beside Europe: +1.

leader.8.why: Whether the chief executive stands above parties: corporatist and strong-leader camps say yes; parliamentary-liberal and party-based camps accept partisan leaders.

notes.STC: Salazar led a regime of 'no parties', the União Nacional being a non-party; Dollfuss and Vargas similarly set the leader above parties: +2.
notes.NAS: Falange called itself a movement, not a party, with a Jefe above factions, though the Falange was itself the party: +1.
notes.HF: Washington's Farewell Address deplored party spirit, but Hamilton and Adams led the Federalist Party: 0.
notes.COA: Competitive authoritarian leaders run through a dominant party and use its machinery: -1.

economy.steering.7.why: Licence-free small business is a deregulatory claim; corporatist and developmentalist states regulate entry, while libertarian camps oppose all licensing.

notes.CRA: Permissionless enterprise, including anonymous digital commerce, is the cypherpunk premise: +3.
notes.STC: Estado Novo's condicionamento industrial required state authorisation to open or expand industry: -1.
notes.SUL: Licences and permits are patronage assets distributed to loyalists: -1.
notes.HF: Hamilton's commercial republic encouraged private enterprise with few entry barriers: +1.

power.checks.2.-2: CO LIF SF RF TRA PIP
power.checks.2.why: Unlimited tenure for a capable leader is the practice of personal and authoritarian regimes; liberal, feminist and communitarian camps insist on term limits.

notes.SUL: Trujillo, Somoza, Marcos and Mobutu ruled for decades and treated the state as property: +3.
notes.STC: Salazar led Portugal for 36 years with no term limits: +2.
notes.HF: Hamilton (Federalist No. 72) argued against presidential term limits and proposed a tenure 'during good behaviour' at Philadelphia: +1.
notes.COA: Fujimori and Mugabe extended terms by constitutional manipulation: +2.
notes.PIP: Pirates hold that power rotates and should be transparent and accountable: -2.

economy.ownership.7.why: Private property as an inviolable natural right is doctrine for Hamiltonian federalism and libertarians; socialist, nationalist and developmentalist camps subordinate it to social aims.

notes.HF: The Federalist and Marshall's Fletcher v. Peck (1810) make property a protected natural right: +3.
notes.CRA: Strong crypto is for protecting one's holdings from the state: +3.
notes.STC: Catholic social teaching affirms private property but with a social function and state oversight: +1.
notes.SF: Marxist feminism treats private property as a root of class and gender oppression: -2.
notes.NAS: Falange nationalised banks and redistributed land, subordinating property to the nation: -1.

lifestyle.gender.1.why: Same-sex marriage divides rights-based camps from Catholic, Orthodox and nationalist traditionalists; economic and institutional variants have little stake.

notes.STC: Catholic corporatism's God-Fatherland-Family triad defines marriage as man and woman: -3.
notes.EUR: Dugin's neo-Eurasianism and Orthodox traditionalism hold the traditional family sacred; Russian law forbids same-sex marriage: -3.
notes.RF: Radical feminists back gay rights but critique marriage as a patriarchal institution: +1.
notes.CO: Etzioni and Sandel back it, MacIntyre's tradition does not, so communitarians divide: 0.
notes.LIF: Equality before law for all couples extends the liberal feminist case: +2.

distribution.labour.5.why: A statutory pay-ratio cap on managers divides egalitarian-left and social-justice camps from market and property camps.

notes.SF: Socialist feminism targets class and pay hierarchies as well as gender: +2.
notes.CRA: Pay set by private contract beyond state reach is cypherpunk first principle: -3.
notes.HF: Hamilton's republic accepts natural inequality of rewards and fears levelling: -3.
notes.NAS: Falange's 27 points subordinate capital to labour and attack plutocratic excess: +1.
notes.STC: Corporatism seeks class harmony and fixed wages through corporations, not a pay cap: -1.

power.checks.6.-2: COA SUL STC NAS HF EUR
power.checks.6.why: A binding term limit overriding voters is liberal-republican in spirit and rejected by authoritarian leader-centred camps and by Hamilton, who thought re-eligibility keeps good executives.

notes.HF: Federalist No. 72 (Hamilton) argues against presidential ineligibility for re-election as harming stability and incentive: -2.
notes.COA: Fujimori and Mugabe defeated or rewrote term limits: -2.
notes.SUL: Personal rulers hold power for life and see limits as a threat: -2.
notes.PIP: Pirates stress transparency and rotation of power: +2.

law.4.why: Implied or unlimited central powers are the Hamiltonian doctrine and the practice of authoritarian states; liberal, libertarian and digital-rights camps want strictly enumerated powers.

notes.HF: Hamilton's 1791 bank opinion and Marshall's McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) establish implied powers for national ends: +3.
notes.SUL: A personal ruler recognises no constitutional limit on what the state may do: +3.
notes.CRA: Cypherpunks seek to deny the state powers it was never granted: -3.
notes.LIF: Liberal constitutionalism of Mill and Wollstonecraft makes rights limits on state power: -2.

world.5.why: Minimal involvement abroad is isolationist neutrality; imperial and great-power camps reject it while internationalist camps prefer engagement.

notes.STC: Salazar kept Portugal neutral in WWII and aloof from Europe's quarrels, keeping to its empire: +2.
notes.EUR: Eurasianism's whole geopolitics is a great-power civilisational contest, not abstention: -2.
notes.NAS: Falange's imperial vocation and Hispanidad claim a world role: -2.
notes.HF: Washington's Farewell Address urged avoiding entanglements, though Hamilton favoured a strong navy and active diplomacy: +1.

economy.ownership.2.why: State ownership of strategic industries is developmentalist and nationalist doctrine; property-first and libertarian camps oppose it.

notes.IS: CEPAL-era Latin America built state enterprises like Petrobras and the national banks to industrialise: +2.
notes.NAS: Falange's 27 points call for nationalising banking and key public services: +2.
notes.STC: Corporatist Portugal left industry in private hands under state supervision (condicionamento industrial): -1.
notes.HF: Hamilton's Bank of the United States was part-private and he preferred private enterprise under state patronage: -2.

elites.rank.4.why: Abolishing hereditary titles is a republican-egalitarian measure; traditionalist and dynastic camps are lukewarm to hostile.

notes.HF: The US Constitution (Art. I, 9) bans titles of nobility and Hamilton defends this in The Federalist No. 84: +2.
notes.SUL: Somoza's and Trujillo's dynasties passed power and property by inheritance: -1.
notes.STC: Corporatist and Habsburg-leaning Austria and Portugal respected tradition and hierarchy: -1.
notes.EUR: Eurasian traditionalism honours imperial hierarchy and heritage: -1.

liberty.privacy.1.why: A judicial-warrant requirement for surveillance is doctrine for crypto-anarchists and pirates and a standard liberal safeguard, but authoritarian regimes spy at will.

notes.CRA: The Cypherpunk Manifesto holds that privacy is necessary for an open society and must be guaranteed technically: +3.
notes.PIP: Pirates campaign against warrantless surveillance and data retention: +3.
notes.STC: The PIDE secret police monitored mail and phones without warrants: -2.
notes.CO: Etzioni accepts court-warranted surveillance for security: +1.

power.local.4.why: National legal uniformity versus local variation: centralisers (authoritarian, nationalist, Hamiltonian) agree, localist communitarians and decentralising libertarians disagree.

notes.HF: Hamilton and the Federalists wanted national supremacy over state laws, as in Federalist No. 15-22: +2.
notes.CO: Subsidiarity and local community are core communitarian values: -2.
notes.CRA: Competing jurisdictions let individuals exit; crypto-anarchists want fragmentation: -2.
notes.NAS: The Falange demanded a unitary Spain against regional separatisms: +2.
notes.EUR: A multiethnic empire gives regions cultural autonomy but with central sovereignty: 0.

power.pluralism.2.-2: CO LIF SF RF HF CRA
power.pluralism.2.why: Single-force rule is doctrine for national syndicalism and typical of personal and corporatist regimes; pluralist, liberal and digital-democracy camps reject it.

notes.NAS: Falange's 27 points ban party politics and set one national movement to govern, unified with Franco's FET y de las JONS: +3.
notes.STC: Salazar's União Nacional and the Ständestaat's Vaterländische Front replaced parties with a single national organisation: +2.
notes.PIP: Pirate politics rests on open, multi-party competition and direct citizen decisions: -3.
notes.COA: Competitive authoritarians keep multi-party elections while tilting the field, so formally against a single force: -1.
notes.HF: Madison's Federalist No. 10 accepts faction and Hamilton led a party himself: -2.

lifestyle.autonomy.3.why: Decriminalising personal cannabis use is a libertarian and cognitive-liberty position; traditionalist and order-first camps oppose it.

notes.CRA: Cypherpunk libertarianism treats consumption choices as outside state power: +3.
notes.PIP: Pirate parties generally call for decriminalising personal drug use as a rights issue: +2.
notes.STC: Catholic corporatist moral order treats drugs and vice as state business: -2.
notes.TRA: Cognitive and morphological liberty extends to personal substance use: +2.
notes.EUR: Russian Orthodox traditionalism and Russian drug law are strict: -2.

identity.nation.5.why: Compatriots-first is nationalist and communitarian doctrine; universalist, internationalist and transhumanist camps reject giving nationality priority.

notes.NAS: Falange's unity of destiny puts the nation's own people first: +3.
notes.CO: MacIntyre and Sandel argue that obligations arise from membership in particular communities: +2.
notes.TRA: Bostrom's and Hughes's ethics extend moral concern across all persons and even future minds: -2.
notes.SF: Zetkin and Kollontai championed international solidarity of women and workers: -1.
notes.STC: God, Fatherland, Family places the national community first: +2.

liberty.justice.2.why: Rights of the accused from the first moment are liberal due-process doctrine; authoritarian and corporatist regimes detain and interrogate at will.

notes.PIP: Pirate programmes defend due process and fair trial against police overreach: +3.
notes.STC: PIDE held suspects incommunicado without lawyers in Salazar's Portugal: -2.
notes.SUL: A ruler's secret police arrest and torture without legal safeguards: -2.
notes.HF: The Bill of Rights (Fifth and Sixth Amendments) was ratified under Federalist leadership: +1.
notes.LIF: Mill's and Wollstonecraft's liberalism makes legal protections for the individual core: +3.

property.5.why: Wage labour as unfreedom is the socialist claim; liberal, property-first and corporatist camps hold that contract makes wage work free.

notes.SF: Marx and socialist feminists describe wage labour as exploitation, with domestic work as unpaid labour behind it: +2.
notes.NAS: Ledesma and Primo de Rivera attacked capitalism's wage-slavery but kept hierarchy within syndicates: +1.
notes.HF: Hamilton's commercial republic is built on free employment contracts and manufactures: -3.
notes.CRA: Voluntary exchange of labour is free by definition for cypherpunks: -2.
notes.STC: Corporatism treats labour and capital as cooperating partners: -2.

environment.nature.8.why: Loosening environmental rules for investment favours growth-first and market camps, while communitarian, feminist and digital-rights camps oppose it.

notes.IS: CEPAL-era developmentalism put industrialisation first and argued the periphery could not wait on green rules: +1.
notes.HF: Hamilton's commercial-republic plan prized manufactures and growth over restrictions: +1.
notes.CO: Communitarians (Sandel, Putnam) tie community life to stewardship of place: -2.
notes.SF: Ecofeminist and socialist critiques link exploitation of nature and of care labour: -2.
notes.CRA: Deregulation fits the minimal-state ethos, though environment is not a cypherpunk topic: +1.

future.1.why: Transhumanism's core claim is that human limits may be exceeded, so it rejects the item doctrinally; Catholic, Orthodox and communitarian camps defend given human nature.

notes.TRA: Huxley, Bostrom and FM-2030 define the movement by overcoming biological limits: -3.
notes.CO: Sandel's The Case Against Perfection argues against genetic enhancement as hubris: +2.
notes.STC: Catholic doctrine on natural law opposes remaking human nature: +2.
notes.RF: Firestone's Dialectic of Sex wants artificial reproduction to free women from biology: -2.
notes.EUR: Dugin attacks transhumanism as the culmination of Western liberal modernity: +2.

change.means.8.why: Permission-only strikes and protests is the order-first position of authoritarian and corporatist regimes; liberal, feminist and digital-rights camps hold that protest is a right.

notes.STC: Estado Novo and the Ständestaat banned strikes and made labour disputes subject to state corporations: +3.
notes.PIP: Pirate politics grows from civic protest and open organising, as with ACTA demonstrations: -3.
notes.LIF: Suffragist and later feminist movements won rights by unpermitted marches and civil disobedience: -2.
notes.COA: Competitive authoritarian regimes require permits and break unpermitted demonstrations: +2.
notes.HF: Federalists suppressed the Whiskey Rebellion and favoured order, though they accepted petitioning rights: +1.
